newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia steps up war of words with NATO.
newsitem.headline: Russia steps up war of words with NATO.

text.p: Russia has stepped up the war of words over NATO's eastward expansion plans and, in a change of emphasis, is warning that enlargement will undermine President Boris Yeltsin's already shaky position.

In clearly coordinated moves, Yeltsin, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais have taken the stand to condemn NATO's plans to take in countries from the former Warsaw Pact.
The Kremlin is turning up the volume on the eve of a trip to Washington by Chernomyrdin, just as it did before a summit in Lisbon last December where NATO enlargement was to be discussed.

Moscow has long argued that enlargement of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation would threaten its security and open new divisions in Europe. It is now drawing attention to the threat to Yeltsin and the risk of instability in Russia.
"It is hard to explain to the Russians. We are all members of the post-war generation and NATO was our enemy for 50 years," Chernomyrdin said in a television interview on Sunday.
"We were told that NATO was our enemy and suddenly NATO is approaching our borders."
In a separate interview published in the Washington Post on Tuesday, Chernomyrdin said: "I am worried about Russia... Developments in Russia could take an ominous turn."

Chubais spelled out similar fears at a meeting of the World Economic Forum in the Swiss mountain resort of Davos on Monday, one day after Yeltsin reiterated Moscow's opposition to NATO expansion in talks with French President Jacques Chirac.
Chubais said a NATO decision to admit Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic would "bring wonderful arguments to the Russian communists and nationalists".

"It is just what they want. It will make them much stronger," Chubais told a Davos news conference, warning that unless NATO made a binding agreement not to move troops and nuclear weapons close to Russia's borders "it would be the worst political mistake made by the West for 50 years."
Yeltsin defeated a communist challenger in last July's presidential election, but nationalists and communists remain a force to be reckoned with in Russian politics.
Their threat cannot be entirely dismissed, particularly because of the 66-year-old president's persistent health problems since his heart surgery last November.
Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov, a possible presidential challenger if Yeltsin had to step down early, also stepped up the rhetoric on Tuesday.
"Russia is a strong enough country to take adequate measures of a defensive nature and not allow the expansion of NATO to the east," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.

NATO enlargement is something of a gift for Yeltsin's opponents, who condemn it fiercely. Almost all Russians oppose or fear NATO plans and it is easy to attack the president for failing to stop them.
Yeltsin faces an almost no-win situation. NATO has made clear that although they want to take account of Russia's fears and do not want to alienate Moscow, enlargement will go ahead.
Yeltsin's best hope appears to be to delay NATO expansion as long as possible and to win as many concessions as he can from his allies in the West.

Shifting attention to the danger to Yeltsin appears to be one way for Moscow to remind Western governments of the risk of instability in Russia and Europe if expansion goes ahead -- something which enlargement is supposed to avoid.
The Kremlin can play on suggestions at home and abroad that sacked security adviser Alexander Lebed could come to power if Yeltsin was unable to govern and an election were called early.

That would have a huge influence on foreign policy. Lebed, a former paratroop commander widely regarded as a political maverick, has made contradictory statements on subjects including foreign relations.
Yeltsin's opponents have quickly picked up on the Kremlin's change of emphasis.

"NATO's expansion eastwards is the result of the policy of Yeltsin and (former Foreign Minister Andrei) Kozyrev, who supported this at the time," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told reporters on Tuesday.
"Now they oppose NATO because they say they are concerned about the possibility of the left opposition coming to power.

"They feel in their bones that if they allow Russia to disintegrate and NATO to expand eastwards there would be such mass protest that they will never keep power. What they say now is in fact a plea for support from the West".
